title: Crosby to insure autonomous agent legal work: professional liability insurance for AI agents
pub: LinkedIn (Daniels, primary); Artificial Lawyer (trade-press report); X (Golan, commentary)
author: Ryan Daniels · Nir Golan · Richard Tromans

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts selective, risk-bounded deployment rather than wholesale lawyer replacement, explicitly preserving lawyers in some review loops. It materially extends the cluster by identifying professional-liability insurance as a trust and differentiation mechanism that could enable autonomous delivery for lower-risk outputs, while recognising uncertain client acceptance and regulatory scrutiny.
qs: > Feels like a way to earn trust (ie our agents do a really good job and we stand behind them like a human lawyer), differentiate, take that big step of seemingly removing the lawyer from some of the output review (probably low risk outputs that they get the highest eval scores on) and going full autonomous.
they're \*not\* saying they will remove lawyers from all the review loops (which is how I'm sure some clients and lawyers will interpret this).

kp.k: Crosby proposes insuring agents to enable autonomous legal work
kp.d: In his July 2026 announcement, Crosby CEO Ryan Daniels describes taking out professional liability insurance for agents as the firm's next step toward autonomous legal work, claiming Crosby is among the first law firms to attempt this. This is an announced initiative rather than evidence of an operational insured service; Artificial Lawyer reports that the insurance company involved has not yet been identified.
qs: We are starting on the next chapter of Crosby: taking out professional liability insurance for our agents, so that they can do autonomous legal work.
We are one of the first law firms to attempt this.
(Although, they have not outlined which insurance company will help with this, yet.)

kp.k: Universal human verification remains current practice, not future intent
kp.d: Daniels states that Crosby's lawyers currently review every output, but predicts this will become unnecessary following improvements in agents over the preceding few months. The document supplies no performance measurements supporting that prediction. Golan interprets the announcement as removing review from certain outputs, not eliminating lawyers from every review loop; his suggestion that these would probably be low-risk, high-scoring outputs is explicitly speculative.
qs: Today, our lawyers review every single work output. As agents have improved in leaps over the last few months, it's become clear this won't be necessary in the future.
(probably low risk outputs that they get the highest eval scores on)
they're \*not\* saying they will remove lawyers from all the review loops (which is how I'm sure some clients and lawyers will interpret this).

kp.k: Autonomy changes the rationale for allocating professional liability
kp.d: Artificial Lawyer argues that comprehensive human verification leaves responsibility with the reviewing lawyer and firm, making special insurance for the agent unnecessary. By contrast, its hypothetical of delivering an entire agent-completed matter without review frames the agent as functionally equivalent to a lawyer or associate requiring insurance. This is the report's interpretation of professional responsibility, not a documented regulatory determination that an agent legally becomes a lawyer.
qs: Because the human lawyer carries the responsibility for checking each response, and then so does the firm as a whole.

But, if you then say 'we trust our agent to do a whole matter' and we will just send you the results 'as is', or perhaps allow you to connect to our platform and also just accept those agent-derived answers from within our business, then this moves into new territory.
The agent *de facto* becomes 'a lawyer' in its own right, and thus needs to be insured as such.

kp.k: Evaluation and regulatory engagement accompany the proposed transition
kp.d: Daniels says Crosby will continue working over the next few months with auditors to define evaluations and with bar associations, state regulators and insurance providers. These are planned activities, not completed evaluations or regulatory approvals. Golan anticipates regulatory issues from the move toward autonomy, without identifying specific rules or resolutions.
qs: Over the next few months, we'll continue working closely with auditors to define evals, as well as with bar associations, state regulators, and insurance providers.
Very provocative (love it) and Ryan knows this hence the discussions with regulators, bar associations, insurers etc as this will trigger regulatory issues.

kp.k: Insurance is framed as client trust and market differentiation
kp.d: Golan interprets insurance as a way for Crosby to stand behind agent-delivered work as it would a human lawyer's work, earn client trust and differentiate an AI-native firm. He characterizes client acceptance of autonomous legal delivery as a bet, rather than reporting demonstrated demand or acceptance.
qs: they plan to insure the work the autonomous agents do, ie to get clients to trust the work/output created and delivered by the agent like a human lawyer.
Feels like a way to earn trust (ie our agents do a really good job and we stand behind them like a human lawyer), differentiate
Another bet is being taken here on how clients will respond to this big step towards end to end autonomous legal work.

kp.k: Existing AI insurance provides precedents, but agents extend scope
kp.d: Artificial Lawyer reports that Orbital obtained underwriting for some AI outputs in UK residential property transactions and launched its own small law firm, while Corgi also offers AI insurance. The report distinguishes Crosby's proposed agent-focused coverage from these precedents, interpreting it as a deeper shift toward treating agents as firm associates and as a signal of confidence in their outputs.
qs: The UK's Orbital got an insurance company to underwrite some of its AI outputs for residential property transactions.
It's also become something of a NewMod, with the launch of its own mini-law firm.
And, more generally, startup Corgi is offering AI insurance as well.
insuring an agent is implicitly saying that you are treating that agent as an associate of the law firm

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Daniels announces plans to insure Crosby's agents for autonomous legal work and predicts that universal human review will become unnecessary; Tromans and Golan interpret the implications differently.
pts.d: Crosby's CEO Ryan Daniels says its lawyers currently review every output, but recent agent improvements make him confident that this will not remain necessary. He announces an attempt to obtain professional liability insurance to enable autonomous legal work, rather than reporting an already operational insured service. Richard Tromans's trade-press analysis interprets agent insurance as treating an agent like a law-firm associate and shifting beyond the model in which a lawyer verifies every response and carries responsibility. His examples of delivering whole matters or platform answers without verification are hypothetical interpretations, not specific Crosby commitments. Nir Golan interprets the announcement more narrowly as removing review from certain outputs, not eliminating every lawyer review loop. Golan suggests insurance could earn client trust, differentiate Crosby and market its end-to-end agentic service; he also predicts regulatory issues.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal basis is Daniels's account of Crosby's workflow and recent agent improvement, supplemented by insurance precedents and commentary rather than reported performance measurements.
pts.d: Daniels offers a first-party qualitative assessment of agent progress and a description of current universal lawyer verification. No accuracy figures, evaluation results, autonomous-work outcomes or insurance terms are supplied. Work with auditors to define evaluations is prospective or continuing, not evidence of a completed benchmark or verification regime. Tromans cites Orbital's insurance for some residential-property AI outputs and Corgi's broader AI insurance offering as precedents, while distinguishing Crosby's agent-focused proposal. He notes that Crosby has not identified an insurer. Golan's suggestion that autonomy will concern low-risk, high-scoring outputs is explicitly conjectural, not a disclosed selection policy or measured result.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The July 2026 announcement describes a transition under development, with stakeholder work over the following months and no specified launch date for autonomous delivery.
pts.d: Daniels contrasts current review of every output with an unspecified future in which that will not be necessary, attributing the change to improvements over the preceding few months. He plans continued work with auditors, bar associations, state regulators and insurers over the next few months; he does not report completed coverage or regulatory approval. Tromans's argument for special agent insurance is conditional on relying directly on agent work rather than a lawyer checking everything before delivery. Golan cautions against reading the announcement as removal of all lawyer review and speculates that the initial scope may be low-risk outputs with the highest evaluation scores.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The proposed change affects Crosby's lawyers and clients directly, with insurers, auditors and legal regulators involved in enabling and assessing autonomous delivery.
pts.d: Crosby's lawyers could move away from verifying every output, although neither a staffing reduction nor the complete removal of lawyer oversight is announced. Clients would potentially receive some agent-generated legal work without individual lawyer verification, with insurance intended, in Golan's interpretation, to support trust. Crosby could differentiate itself as an agentic legal-service provider. Insurers would be asked to cover agent-related professional liability, auditors would help define evaluations, and bar associations and state regulators would engage with the proposal's regulatory implications. Tromans frames this as a broader development for the legal sector, but the document does not establish a profession-wide adoption forecast, a specified practice-area scope for Crosby, or client acceptance.
